[WP] They came, they saw, they let us do our own thing..

One by one, they filed in and took their seats at the conference table. Some smirked; most weren't even awake. A secretary muttered something into a cup of coffee.

"Do we really need to do this?" A young man at the head of the table wore one of those smirks. By his dress and hair, nobody would have guessed at his actual success, unless they knew better. And everybody in the room knew better.

"Protocol," muttered a crisply-dressed woman with a five-o'-clock shadow. Finding herself suddenly, she perked up, "But we have doughnuts!" The secretary finished his conversation with the cup of brew, and excused himself to the snack table. The room remained silent, save the shuffling of papers and whir of laptops powering on. She yawned, "Sorry, I was out at the community theater all night."

A government man chuckled, "That explains the makeup, ma'am." Polite chuckles were passed around the room, unlike the doughnut box greedily guarded by a practically-zombified secretary. "Okay, let's get on with this so we can get back to work. What do we got?"

The successful-but-street-dressed young man went straight into presentation mode, "It's a new social media website. It's gaining some intermittent traction. We show peaks of activity where content isn't allowed on our platform, a little bellyaching about politics, and lots of criticism about us."

"So, malcontents, liberals, political types, and people looking to start fresh by their own rules," appended the pretty lady with the dashing facial hair. "Is it anything we need to worry about, and can we use it?"

"That's what we're here to establish," the CEO remarked dryly.

"I know just who you mean. Intel doesn't show anything about extremist groups, no hackers, nothing illicit. It can be a little low-brow, but they seem harmless enough according to our logs," the government man tapped the "down" arrow on his laptop. "It's just blackjack and hookers."

"Blackjack and hookers?" The secretary spoke through a mouth full of doughnut, on the way back to his seat.

"It's a reference to a cartoon comedy show that used to be on television," the t-shirt-and-jeans CEO explained, "A meme, kind of." There was a buzzer as somebody very professional-looking marched in with some papers, whispered in the young CEO's ear, and departed. People shuffled awkwardly in their seats, and he thumbed through the delivery. "Maybe we should get down to it," he announced, suddenly perky, "since it's the weekend and we have other work to do anyway."

"Yeah, you interrupted my fishing."

"You fish in LA? Want a doughnut?"

"Don't ask about that. And I'm sure Catherine would like to wash off her beard." A moment's pause, "Frank will fall asleep with his mouth full if we take too long."

"No doughnut."

A Windows startup tune from the nineties interjected in its own way, as the secretary opened his laptop. "Dear God, man! Can't you get your people some new equipment?" Frank looked up like a deer caught in headlights at the sound of the government man's voice projected in his direction.

"Mffwhat? I like phish 'puter."

"He uses his own gear, and he doesn't ever connect to the wifi," the CEO explained. "Okay... So... We'll maybe have a few participants on board, maybe replicate some of our operations on the primary site, to get established. If it catches on, then we'll already be in the door."

"We already have agents logging everything, boring as it is to us." The government man shook his head, "We'll just keep the logger running."

"So, no new operations, no marketing, nothing?"

"Not yet, Catherine. Just let them have their own club. They'll probably still participate with us anyway, and maybe they'll be useful one day."

"That fits with our program just fine. They'll slip up if there's anything to catch, since they can say whatever they want there. We're good at fishing. Can I smoke?"

"Don't they talk about monetizing posts? We could totally own that! And I thought you can't smoke. Regulations or something?"

"Shit, Catherine. Regulations. Psh. I'll wait. Anything else to add?"

"Nothing here. And no. It needs legs before we try to leverage it for anything, even monetized posts. Maybe later. We can meet again in six months." The CEO stood and stretched, "We'll just leave them be. I'll see you guys Monday." He organized his papers, and briskly marched out of the room; a model of purpose and gravitas textured with materials sampled from some college kid.

Frank nearly choked on his doughnut. "That's it?"

"That's it! Welcome aboard, and see you Monday," Catherine chirped with a wink.

As she made her way out, and Frank fumbled to get his over-prepared materials together, the government man groaned, "Fuck it," and lit a cigarette. "If you tell anyone, I'll bug your house and post pics of you taking a shit."

Thusly, the meeting concluded.

Hello Criminologists! I've noticed a lack of podcast discussion in this subreddit, so to amend that I shall take it upon myself to provide a reference in podcasts to check out!

A problem with Criminology is that there is not a subculture of "Pop Criminology" (as there is Pop Science), so to supplement the academics, I've also included some social science podcasts that are not so crime-focused, but do have crime topics. Well without further ado:

Academic Criminology

  • NW-SCC CRJ208 - Introduction to Criminology Distance Education. This is a video lecture featuring seventeen episodes of 50-minute segments that teaches the basics of Criminology. Features a lecturer and powerpoint slides.

Criminology/Criminal Justice Discussions & Pop Crime

  • Criminal Justice Discussions with David Onek. Every episode of this podcasts features guest speakers who hold conversations on relevant Criminal Justice topics. Examples of such guest speakers are police chiefs, a professor of the Berkeley law school, the president of the NAACP, etc.

  • Criminal Justice Research Podcast from the National Institute of Justice. This podcast from the NIJ features numerous brief discussions (usually under 10 minutes) on research and new improvements of the criminal justice system.

  • SAGE Criminology. Features authors who have written articles that deal with Criminology and has them discuss their articles. Every episode features a different author and provides a diverse collection of issues or improvements in the CJS.

  • UCT Centre of Criminology. Features lectures, interviews, and discussions on criminological topics with a variety of guest speakers.

  • Inside the FBI. Discusses some of the most interesting cases handled by the FBI, including scams, murders, white collar corruption, and gangs. This podcast provides the community insight into what the FBI does, such as how they investigate or how they apprehend criminals.

  • Its a Crime With Margaret McLean. Every episode is around 1 hour 36 minutes long with a variety of topics including: serial killers, organizational crime, interviews with former police, conspiracies, psychics, popular crime trials, forensics, movies, and far more.

Social Science Discussions

  • Social Science Bites. Has some discussions on criminology, inequality, disgust (deviance?), death, morality, and behavioral studies.

  • Thinking Allowed. Provides many discussions of crime, criminology, and inequality in numerous episodes. This podcast is expansive. There are so many topics that fall under social science and so many episodes here that it would be difficult to find this podcast uninteresting.

Well, that's all I got! Please recommend anything that I might have missed!

A rant revisited

I think the most supreme problem of textbook writing nowadays is the tendency to try to cram "everything" into one book; many textbooks try to appear comprehensive, but come short. A jack of all trades, a master in none. Now what does cramming do to a textbook?

  1. Giant pages to accommodate more text.

  2. An attempt to "balance" different ideas by giving each chapter the same number of pages.

  3. An overbreadth of names, institutions, locations, statistics, etc.

  4. Overbroad scope, too cautious to focus in on one theme.

Now I shall explain the bullets deeper:

I think its common sense to understand that textbooks are bigger than usual books. One page of a textbook can accommodate four times as much text as a page of paperback novel text. Furthermore, textbooks strive to stay within a 300-700 page range when their page-content is already so high. Trying to read a page with so much text in the span of nine weeks (the average semester of a US university) is a challenge. Trying to read as much as five textbooks during the same period is hell. "Let's just bombard students with too much information while they simultaneously try to speedily progress through their education," is what I could imagine textbook publishers saying.

The balancing is also an issue; not all ideas are created equal. I think it would be sufficient to say that some ideas require more depth and explanation than others. Trying to allot the same amount of importance to each idea means either filling a chapter with fluff or repetitive writing or cutting off a topic too short. The problem of the former is that students cannot predict whether the next sentence, paragraph, or page is going to be irrelevant or not, so they suffer through a text without progressing even marginally. The problem of the latter is that when larger concepts are cut short, then so too is understanding.

Just a side-note, but I absolutely loathe the pacing used in textbooks. As I described earlier, textbook pages are massive and then students are assigned 30-60 pages (sometimes a day!) that equates to about 90-120 pages of a novel. Its not paced right to sync with a nine-week course.

As for the noun-abuse, I think its fine if a textbook uses examples. I do not find it fine when they namedrop without adequate background of the person's idea being discussed nor do I find it fine when there are hundreds of examples used in a single chapter. The problem with this is that students will gloss over names or examples simply because the idea is abandoned within the proceeding paragraph (and rest of the text). Examples should be meaningful, not just there. Did you know that the American Association of Donkey Sports found a 93% boom in cocaine use among donkeys in the 1950's? Well who the fuck cares, because we're going to we're just going to lecture upon cocaine use in general and never talk about the AADS ever again.

And lastly: scope. I don't think textbooks should "encompass" all of the ideas of a subject, because they do so poorly. I would rather read a 100-200 page essay or book on a very narrow focus than a 300-700 textbook on a broad focus. Specialization > Generalization.

Well that's all I have for now. Another semester has ended and I'm just re-annoyed with the system.
